source_text: XVIII. Εἷς δέ τις τῶν ἐν ὑπεροχῇ καὶ δόξῃ κοσμικῇ καὶ Λέπιδος σὺν αὐτῷ εἶπον· Μὴ κρᾶξε, Πιόνιε. ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· Καὶ μὴ βιάζου· πῦρ ἄναψον καὶ [ἕτοιμοι — scan ἑαυτοῖς] ἀναβαίνομεν. Τερέντιος δέ τις ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄχλου ἀνέκραξεν· Οἴδατε ὅτι οὗτος καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἀνασοβεῖ ἵνα μὴ θύσωσιν; λοιπὸν οὖν στεφάνους ἐπετίθεσαν αὐτοῖς· οἱ δὲ διασπῶντες αὐτοὺς ἀπέρριπτον. ὁ δὲ δημόσιος εἱστήκει τὸ εἰδωλόθυτον κρατῶν· οὐ μέντοι ἐτόλμησεν ἐγγύς τινος προσελθεῖν, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸς ἐνώπιον πάντων κατέφαγεν αὐτό. κραζόντων δὲ αὐτῶν· Χριστιανοί ἐσμεν, μὴ εὑρίσκοντες τὸ τί ποιήσωσιν αὐτοῖς ἀνέπεμψαν αὐτοὺς πάλιν εἰς τὴν φυλακήν, ὁ δὲ ὄχλος ἐνέπαιζέ τε καὶ ἐρράπιζεν αὐτούς. καὶ τῇ Σαβίνῃ τις λέγει· Σὺ εἰς τὴν πατρίδα σου οὐκ ἠδύνω ἀποθανεῖν; ἡ δὲ εἶπεν· Τίς ἐστιν ἡ πατρίς μου; ἐγὼ Πιονίου ἀδελφή εἰμι. πρὸς δὲ Ἀσκληπιάδην Τερέντιος ὁ τότε ἐπιτελῶν τὰ κυνήγια εἶπεν· Σὲ αἰτήσομαι κατάδικον εἰς τὰς μονομάχους φιλοτιμίας τοῦ υἱοῦ μου. ὃ δὲ Ἀσκληπιάδης πρὸς αὐτόν· Οὐ φοβεῖς με ὧν τούτῳ. καὶ οὕτως εἰσήχθησαν εἰς τὴν φυλακήν. καὶ εἰσιόντι τῷ Πιονίῳ εἰς τὴν φυλακὴν εἷς τῶν διωγμιτῶν ἔκρουσε κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς μεγάλως ὥστε τραυματίσαι αὐτόν· ὁ δὲ ἡσύχασεν. αἱ χεῖρες δὲ τοῦ πατάξαντος αὐτὸν καὶ τὰ πλευρὰ ἐφλέγμαναν ὥστε μόλις αὐτὸν ἀναπνεῖν. εἰσελθόντες δὲ ἐδόξασαν τὸν θεὸν ὅτι ἔμειναν ἐν ὀνόματι Χριστοῦ ἀβλαβεῖς καὶ οὐκ ἐκράτησεν αὐτῶν ὁ ἐχθρὸς οὐδὲ Εὐκτήμων ὁ ὑποκριτής, καὶ διετέλουν ἐν ψαλμοῖς καὶ εὐχαῖς ἐπιστηρίζοντες ἑαυτούς. ἐλέγετο δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα ὅτι ἠξίωσεν ὁ Εὐκτήμων ἀναγκασθῆναι ἡμᾶς, καὶ ὅτι αὐτὸς ἀπήνεγκε τὸ [ἴδιον — scan ὀίέδιον, sense unclear: his portion] εἰς τὸ Νεμεσεῖον, ὃ καὶ μετὰ φαγεῖν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ὀπτηθὲν ἠθέλησεν ὅλον τὸν οἶκον ἀποφέρειν. ὡς ἐγκατάγελαστον αὐτὸν διὰ τὴν ἐπιορκίαν γενέσθαι, ὅτε ὤμοσε τὴν τοῦ αὐτοκράτορος τύχην καὶ τὰς Νεμέσεις στεφανωθεὶς μὴ εἶναι Χριστιανὸς μηδὲ ὡς οἱ λοιποὶ παραλιπεῖν τι τῶν πρὸς τὴν ἐξάρνησιν.
pass_a_gloss: One of those in worldly eminence and glory, and Lepidus with him, said: Do not cry out, Pionius. And he to him: Do not force; light a fire, and being ready we go up. And a certain Terentius from the crowd shouted out: Do you know that this man also stirs up the others so that they will not sacrifice? Then they kept putting garlands on them, but they kept tearing them off and throwing them away. And the public man stood holding the idol-meat; he did not dare to come near anyone, but himself ate it up before all. And while they were crying, We are Christians, since they did not find what to do to them they sent them up again into prison, and the crowd both mocked and slapped them. And someone says to Sabina: Could you not die in your own homeland? And she said: What is my homeland? I am the sister of Pionius. And to Asclepiades Terentius, the one then managing the hunts, said: I shall request you as condemned for my son's gladiatorial show. And Asclepiades to him: You do not frighten me with this. And so they were led into prison. And as Pionius was entering into prison one of the pursuers struck him hard on the head so as to wound him; but he kept quiet. And the hands and sides of the one who struck him became inflamed so that he could scarcely breathe. And having entered they glorified God because they remained unharmed in the name of Christ and the enemy did not get hold of them, nor Euctemon the pretender, and they continued in psalms and prayers strengthening themselves. And it was said after these things that Euctemon requested that we be compelled, and that he himself carried his portion into the Nemeseion, and after eating roasted meat from it he wanted to carry it off for his whole house. So he became a laughingstock on account of his perjury, when having been garlanded he swore by the fortune of the emperor and the Nemeses that he was not a Christian nor, like the rest, would he leave out anything toward denial.
pass_b_english: One man of worldly rank and glory, with Lepidus beside him, said, Do not shout, Pionius.
And he answered him, Do not force me; kindle the fire, and we go up ready.
Then a certain Terentius shouted from the crowd, Do you know that this man is also stirring up the rest not to sacrifice?
So they kept setting garlands upon them, but the prisoners kept tearing them off and casting them away.
And the public officer stood holding the idol-meat, yet he did not dare to come close to any of them, but ate it himself in front of them all.
And as they kept crying, We are Christians, and the authorities found nothing further to do with them, they sent them back again to prison, while the crowd mocked them and struck them with the hand.
And someone said to Sabina, Could you not have died in your own homeland?
And she said, What is my homeland?
I am the sister of Pionius.
And to Asclepiades, Terentius, who was then in charge of the beast-hunts, said, I shall demand you as a condemned man for my son's munificent gladiatorial show.
And Asclepiades said to him, You do not frighten me with that.
And so they were brought into the prison.
And as Pionius was going into the prison, one of his pursuers struck him a great blow upon the head, so that he wounded him, but Pionius remained silent.
And the hands and the sides of the man who struck him swelled with inflammation, so that the man could scarcely breathe.

And once inside, they glorified God that they had remained unharmed in the name of Christ, and that the enemy had gained no hold upon them, nor Euctemon the pretender, and they continued in psalms and prayers, strengthening themselves.

And it was reported afterward that Euctemon had demanded that we be forced, and that he himself carried his portion into the temple of Nemesis, and after eating some of it roasted he wished to carry the rest away for his whole household.

Thus he became a laughingstock because of his false oath, since with a garland upon him he had sworn by the fortune of the emperor and by the Nemeses that he was no Christian and that, like the rest, he would omit nothing belonging to denial.

choices.why: masculine substantive without office named points to the civic attendant handling the meat, not a private executioner, and the context is holding and eating idol-meat before the crowd
in a persecution and gladiatorial context it denotes staged hunts with beasts, which fits Terentius threatening condemnation to the shows
genitive with gladiatorial language denotes a sponsor's lavish exhibition for his son, not private ambition
